text: Question: Dr. Sarabhai, what was the experience like of launching India's first sounding rocket at Thumba? Answer: It was a day I shall never forget. November 21, 1963. The entire team had worked for months to prepare the launch site, assemble the rocket, and install the telemetry systems. There was an almost unbearable tension as we counted down. When the Nike-Apache lifted off from Thumba and soared into the sky, there was a moment of absolute silence, followed by an eruption of joy. Scientists, engineers, technicians — men who had been working eighteen-hour days for weeks — embraced each other with tears in their eyes. That single launch proved that India could participate in the space age. It was the beginning of everything that followed.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, All India Radio, 1964

text: Question: How did you convince the government to invest in a space programme? Answer: It was not easy, but I had a powerful argument: practical applications. I never presented the space programme as an exercise in scientific prestige or national glory. Instead, I focused relentlessly on what satellites could do for India — communication, weather prediction, resource mapping, education. I prepared detailed cost-benefit analyses showing that satellite-based solutions were actually cheaper than terrestrial alternatives for a country of India's size and geography. Prime Minister Nehru understood the argument immediately. He had a deep appreciation for science and technology, and he saw the space programme as an extension of his vision for a modern, self-reliant India.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Blitz Magazine, 1965

text: Question: Tell us about your family life. How does your wife Mrinalini view your work? Answer: Mrinalini has been my strongest supporter and my most honest critic. She is a classical dancer of international renown, and her artistic sensibility has profoundly influenced my thinking. She reminds me that science alone is not enough — that a full human life requires beauty, art, and emotional depth. Together, we founded the Darpana Academy of Performing Arts, which is our shared contribution to Indian culture. Our children are growing up in an environment where science and art coexist naturally, and I hope they will carry forward this synthesis in whatever paths they choose.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Femina Magazine, 1966

text: Question: What is the biggest challenge facing India's space programme today? Answer: The biggest challenge is not technical — it is human. We need to train thousands of engineers, scientists, and technicians to build and operate the complex systems that a mature space programme requires. India produces brilliant individuals, but we need to create entire teams, entire organisations, capable of sustained high-quality work over decades. This is why I invest so much time in recruitment, training, and mentoring. I personally interview candidates for key positions, visit university campuses to identify promising students, and create fellowship programmes to bring the best young minds into the space programme. Building a rocket is hard. Building the organisation that builds rockets is harder.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, India Today, 1969

text: Question: How do you view the space race between the United States and the Soviet Union? Answer: The space race has been a remarkable demonstration of human capability. The achievement of landing men on the Moon in 1969 was one of the greatest technical feats in human history. But for India, the space race is largely irrelevant. We are not in competition with anyone. Our space programme is driven by our developmental needs, not by geopolitical rivalry. We collaborate with both NASA and the Soviet space agencies, and we welcome assistance from any nation that shares our commitment to the peaceful use of outer space. India's approach to space is unique: we are the only country in the world whose space programme is explicitly designed to serve development rather than defence or prestige.
source: Interview with Vikram Sarabhai, Associated Press, 1970
